NFL Second-Half and Quarter Lines: How They're Actually Priced

Published September 17, 2026 · 9 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

A full-game spread and total get most of the attention on an NFL Sunday, but every one of those games is also being priced in pieces: a first-half line posted before kickoff, a second-half line that opens the moment halftime starts, and — at some books — quarter lines that reset four separate times inside the same 60 minutes. New bettors often assume a second-half spread is just the full-game number cut in proportion to whatever's left on the clock. It isn't, and the gap between that assumption and how books actually build these numbers is where a lot of value gets left on the table, in both directions.

What second-half and quarter lines actually are

A first-half line is posted alongside the full-game spread and total before kickoff and covers only what happens in the first two quarters; it settles at halftime regardless of how the second half plays out. A second-half line doesn't exist until halftime arrives — it's built and posted fresh once the first half is complete, using the actual score, game flow, and any new information (an injury, a blowout developing, weather turning) that's accumulated since the opening kick. Quarter lines work the same way in miniature: each of the four quarters gets its own spread and total, priced only once the previous quarter has ended.

The key distinction is that the full-game line is a single forecast made once, twelve-plus hours ahead of kickoff in many cases, while half and quarter lines are repriced at each break using real, in-game information the full-game number never had access to. That's what makes them a genuinely different market, not just a fraction of the same one.

Why a second-half line isn't just "half" of the full-game number

If a full-game total sits at 46.5, a bettor's first instinct might be to expect the second-half total to land somewhere near 23. In practice it's almost always priced a little higher than a straight 50/50 split would suggest, because NFL scoring isn't evenly distributed across two halves. Game script pushes scoring toward the back half more often than not: trailing teams speed up their offense and pass more, leading teams occasionally lean run-heavy in the third quarter before opening back up late, and two-minute-drill situations at the end of the second and fourth quarters compress scoring into short windows. None of that is a hard rule for any single game, but across a large sample, second-half team totals skew modestly higher than first-half team totals on average, and sportsbooks price around that tendency rather than a clean fractional split.

Spreads follow a related logic. A double-digit full-game favorite's second-half spread is rarely just half the original number, because the score at halftime already reflects part of that expected margin. A team favored by 10 that's up 17-3 at the break is being priced for the remaining 30 minutes based on the game state that actually exists, not the pregame forecast that predicted it.

Reality check: half and quarter lines are freshly modeled at every break, not simple arithmetic on the full-game number. Treating them as a fraction of the opening line is a common and costly shortcut.

A worked example: pricing the second half live

Say a full-game line has a home favorite at -7 with a 44 total. At halftime, the home team leads 20-10. The pregame model already "used up" some of that projected -7 margin in the first half; what's left to price is a fresh 30-minute game with a 10-point head start already on the board, current pace, whichever team has the ball to start the third quarter, and any injuries that emerged. A second-half line built off that situation might open the home team around -2.5 or -3 for the second half alone, with a second-half total in the low-to-mid 20s — numbers that have almost no fixed mathematical relationship to the original -7 and 44, because they're answering a completely different, narrower question: what happens in the 30 minutes that are left, given everything now known.

This is also why second-half lines can occasionally look "wrong" relative to the full-game number to a bettor who hasn't been watching closely — they're not supposed to reconcile neatly with a pregame forecast. They're a new forecast.

Quarter lines: smaller samples, bigger swings

Quarter lines take everything about half lines and compress it further. Fifteen minutes of game clock is a small enough sample that a single defensive score, a long kickoff return, a garbage-time touchdown, or a key player leaving with an injury can swing the number sharply from one quarter's line to the next. Books widen quarter-line vig and move quarter numbers more aggressively in response to new information than they do full-game lines, precisely because the smaller sample means each new data point (an early three-and-out, a quick opening-drive score) carries proportionally more weight on what's left to play.

That volatility cuts both ways. It creates opportunities for a bettor who's watching the game closely and reacts faster than a line update lands, but it also means quarter markets punish a slow reaction far more severely than a full-game bet would — a number that was fair thirty seconds ago can be stale after one more offensive snap.

How the vig compares across full-game, half, and quarter markets

MarketTypical liquidityTypical vigRepricing frequency
Full gameHighestStandard (near -110 each side)Set pregame, moves gradually
First halfHighSlightly above standardSet pregame, moves gradually
Second halfModerateAbove standardFreshly built at halftime
Individual quarterLowerWidest of the fourFreshly built at each break

Lower liquidity and a smaller information base generally translate into a wider hold for the book on half and especially quarter markets. That's not a sign the market is "rigged" against these bets — it's the standard tradeoff for a market with fewer bettors, less time to develop consensus pricing, and a narrower sample of game clock behind it. For more on how vig itself is calculated, see our guide on how vig works and break-even win rate.

Common mistakes bettors make with segment lines

The most common mistake is exactly the assumption this guide opened with: expecting a second-half or quarter number to be a clean fraction of the full-game line, then treating any deviation from that fraction as a mispriced number worth attacking. A second mistake is under-adjusting bet sizing for the extra volatility in quarter markets — a stake that's reasonable on a full-game spread can carry meaningfully more variance in a 15-minute window. A third is ignoring which team has the ball, and where, at the exact moment a half or quarter line gets posted; that single piece of context often explains a number that otherwise looks surprising. And a fourth is forgetting that halftime and quarter-break lines move fast once posted — hesitating to confirm a "better" opinion often means betting into a number that's already adjusted to reflect it.

These segment markets sit on top of the same fundamentals that govern full-game lines. If you haven't already, our guides on NFL alternate spreads and totals and closing line value cover related ground worth understanding first.

Frequently asked questions

Do all sportsbooks offer quarter lines, or just halves?

Coverage varies by operator. Nearly every major book offers first-half and second-half lines on NFL games; quarter-by-quarter lines are common but not universal, and some books only post them for higher-profile matchups.

Is the first-half line set the same way as the second-half line?

No. The first-half line is built pregame, alongside the full-game number, using only forecasted information. The second-half line is built fresh at halftime using the actual first-half result and updated game context, which is why the two aren't priced the same way even though both cover 30 minutes of football.

Why does a second-half total sometimes seem high compared to the full-game total?

Because NFL scoring tends to skew modestly toward the second half on average, due to game-script effects like hurry-up offense from trailing teams and end-of-half scoring windows. A second-half total isn't meant to equal roughly half the full-game total; it's priced off second-half scoring patterns specifically.

Are half and quarter lines worth betting for a casual bettor?

They can be, but the wider vig and faster-moving numbers mean they generally reward close attention to the live game more than full-game lines do. A bettor who isn't watching the game unfold in real time typically has less of an edge in these markets than in the pregame full-game line.
